content_html:
A sweet, solvent-like, or chemical odor can come from paint, adhesives, cleaners, refrigerants, overheated plastics, or stored products. Odor alone cannot identify the substance. If it is strong, sudden, irritating, or appears with smoke, heat, or a failing appliance, move away from the area and prioritize ventilation or professional help as appropriate.

Narrow the room without approaching a possible hazard

From a safe distance, determine whether the odor is near recent paint, cleaning products, a garage, heating and cooling equipment, or an electrical appliance. Do not put your face near outlets, machines, or containers to identify it.

Link the timing to recent products or work

Paints, sealants, new furnishings, and some adhesives release volatile compounds for a period. Follow manufacturer ventilation and curing instructions. If the odor grows rather than fades, or causes symptoms, leave the exposure and seek advice.

An overheating appliance changes the priority

A chemical odor with hot plastic, buzzing, discoloration, or a tripped breaker can indicate an electrical fault. Shut down or disconnect from a safe point if you can do so without approaching the hazard, and do not keep testing the equipment before it is checked.

Symptoms or a strong unknown source justify leaving

Headache, dizziness, respiratory irritation, nausea, or an odor filling several rooms is not a reason to keep searching for hours. Move to fresh air and contact emergency services, poison resources, or the appropriate local service based on severity and the suspected product.
